deltas.summary:
The proposition is the danger thesis that anchored public concern about the Large Hadron Collider before its 2008 start, and the examined evidence weighs against it on each of its legs. The claim is an extreme conditional compound: it requires that the LHC produce black holes at all, which presupposes speculative physics in which [[claim:e382b679-7f22-451c-a551-864fc0c798b5|large extra dimensions lower the Planck scale to the TeV range]], a scenario collider and astrophysical constraints have increasingly disfavored and dedicated searches have never confirmed; it requires stability against evaporation, contrary to the strong theoretical expectation that [[claim:fcab83dc-9428-40e2-86dc-457774afaafa|any collider-produced black hole evaporates essentially instantly via Hawking radiation]]; and it requires that [[claim:6a7966e4-5704-4295-adbf-837de96f26cd|a stable trapped black hole accrete matter fast enough to grow and destroy the planet]], the step on which the direct evidence turns.

The peer-reviewed analysis of Giddings and Mangano (https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.3381, Physical Review D 78, 035009 (2008)) grants production and stability for the sake of argument and finds no surviving danger: scenarios in which a trapped black hole could grow dangerously fast are excluded because cosmic rays striking far denser white dwarfs and neutron stars would have produced the same black holes and destroyed those long-lived, well-observed bodies long ago. The observational premise is solid: [[claim:11887800-2f7b-4ac5-99c2-4dc5bb2f7f7a|cosmic rays above LHC energies have struck Earth, the Moon, and dense stars for billions of years]]. Independent work reaches the same verdict, including the CERN-affiliated review by Ellis, Giudice, Mangano, Tkachev, and Wiedemann (https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.3414) and the Casadio, Fabi, and Harms analysis in the warped brane-world framework (https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.2948). A decade and a half of LHC operation, including dedicated CMS and ATLAS searches with no microscopic black hole events, weighs further against production at any reachable scale.

The one credible contrary voice is Plaga's preprint (https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.1415), which constructs a metastable scenario in which black holes accrete at the Eddington limit and evade the astrophysical exclusions; it concedes that the mainstream analyses are technically correct under their assumptions and attributes the different verdicts to different initial assumptions. Giddings and Mangano's published reply (https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.4087) argues the scenario is internally inconsistent, the claimed black hole radius exceeding the Schwarzschild radius for the relevant mass range by many orders of magnitude, and that the white dwarf and neutron star bounds would apply regardless. The literature has not taken the scenario up. For the claim to revive, a derivation would need to show dangerous accretion rates for a stable trapped black hole in a parameter range that survives the compact-star constraints; no published argument presently does.

deltas.text: A microscopic black hole's accretion rate in matter is far too low to grow it significantly on planetary timescales
Neutron stars and white dwarfs surviving primordial black hole absorption bounds microscopic black hole accretion rates
A black hole stable against Hawking evaporation must have a mass of roughly 10^15 grams or more
A microscopic black hole produced in a particle collision could have a velocity low enough to be gravitationally trapped inside Earth
Cosmic ray collisions at energies above the LHC's have struck Earth, the Moon, and dense stars for billions of years without producing dangerous black holes.

deltas.summary: The claim, read as the danger scenario, is rejected by the physics literature: a black hole that is stable enough to persist in Earth and is trapped there accretes ordinary matter far too slowly to grow on any planetary timescale, and no credible analysis has sustained a route from a trapped hole to planetary destruction. The decisive study is Giddings and Mangano's analysis of hypothetical stable TeV-scale black holes, which examined a wide range of gravity scenarios and found, on first-principles accretion physics, that significant growth within the Earth's natural lifetime is excluded; cases in which accretion could act quickly would have had visible consequences for much denser white dwarfs and neutron stars struck by cosmic-ray-produced black holes, and those stars plainly survive. The same conclusion is reached independently by the 2003 LHC Safety Study Group's successors and by a brane-world analysis that set out to test catastrophic growth and found none. A single dissenting line (Rainer Plaga) has argued that within one quantum-mechanical model of black holes a captured hole could accrete at the Eddington limit and remain astrophysically invisible; the specific numerical claims in that argument were challenged as internally inconsistent in a published reply, and its destruction channel is radiation from the accreting hole rather than growth that consumes the planet. The honest reading of the record is that the consensus position is very strongly supported and the dissent is confined to a speculative model framework whose key quantitative step has not survived scrutiny, so the danger scenario is assessed as contradicted rather than merely unsupported, with residual uncertainty acknowledged for physics outside tested models.

deltas.summary:
This is the "nature has already done the experiment" observation at the heart of the LHC safety debate, and its occurrence half is as solid as astronomy gets. The measured cosmic ray spectrum extends far beyond collider energies, so collisions at and above the LHC's scale have indeed taken place, in vast numbers, in [[claim:30900835-d08a-4e1e-994b-26fefe8e21db|Earth's atmosphere]], on [[claim:214766e5-5cce-4f01-a7f4-a4636d7bc069|the Moon's directly exposed surface]], and in [[claim:7393a80b-648a-4293-b407-c8a9f49ae250|white dwarfs and neutron stars throughout their lifetimes]]. No part of that occurrence record is disputed in the scientific literature.

The outcome half is where honest uncertainty enters. The struck bodies are intact, and the two primary safety analyses read that intactness as evidence: Giddings and Mangano's peer-reviewed study of hypothetical stable black holes (https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.3381) rules out dangerous accretion scenarios because black holes produced by cosmic rays on far denser white dwarfs and neutron stars would long ago have catalyzed the decay of those long-lived bodies, and the CERN safety review (https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.3414) reaches the same reading, citing collision rates on Earth, the Sun, and compact stars. The related conclusion that [[claim:d7357393-c216-45e1-92bc-04896a5af2ad|observed white dwarfs and neutron stars exclude dangerous accretion scenarios]] is built directly on this record.

What keeps the verdict at "supported" rather than "verified" is the escape-route caveat, and the safety literature itself flags it: the record strictly shows that above-LHC collisions did not destroy their hosts, and it excludes dangerous lingering black holes only under the standard expectation that a black hole dangerous to a host would remain and damage it. Scenarios in which a produced black hole evaporates essentially instantly via Hawking radiation, escapes its host at near-light speed, or leaves the brane in higher-dimensional models would leave no trace, so [[claim:63a9f088-5de5-4bfc-896f-cc8c0128b9d9|a dangerous black hole could in principle be produced without leaving an observable trace]] cannot be dismissed by the record alone. The one published construction arguing this seriously (Plaga, arXiv:0808.1415) was answered in a published reply finding it internally inconsistent and arguing the compact star bounds apply regardless (arXiv:0808.4087), and the literature has not taken it up. A peer-reviewed demonstration that dangerous production with no observable trace survives those bounds would change this verdict.

Black holes evaporate by emitting Hawking radiation.
Some theoretical models allow black holes to leave stable or long-lived remnants instead of evaporating completely.
Semiclassical Hawking theory describes collider-produced black holes down to the end of their evaporation.

deltas.summary:
Any black hole that could be produced at a particle collider has, in the scenarios that permit production at all, a mass of at most some tens of TeV, and standard theory assigns it a lifetime of order the inverse of the fundamental (Planck) scale, about 10^-27 seconds: it would decay into ordinary particles long before crossing the detector. This is the mainstream expectation and the premise the LHC safety analyses lean on, resting on [[claim:8fd1ca40-9a74-48c5-89a0-1e97dedf213d|black holes evaporating via Hawking radiation]], a standard semiclassical derivation that has never been directly observed for any black hole, together with a general quantum argument that a collider-produced hole carries no conserved charge that could stabilize it, leaving no small parameter to slow the decay.

The credible disagreement is not about the theory far from its limits but about whether semiclassical Hawking theory can be trusted through the final stage of a hole whose whole mass sits near the fundamental scale. If [[claim:71cef434-08e8-4d54-b335-6a6a1f16903c|semiclassical theory fails before a collider-produced hole finishes evaporating]], quantum-gravity corrections could slow or halt the process: the literature contains proposals for stable Planck-mass remnants, for metastable holes (Kuhnel and Sundell), and for a memory-burden effect that suppresses evaporation partway through, with recent work applying the last of these to collider-scale holes in extra-dimensional scenarios. A published dissent by Plaga argued that such scenarios leave a residual risk the astrophysical safety arguments do not close. No dissenting source claims any observation against the claim, and no collider black hole has ever been produced or detected; LHC searches have also found no sign of the extra-dimensional production scenario itself. The expectation that collider holes evaporate essentially instantly is therefore strongly supported but rests on extrapolated theory at exactly the point where its extrapolation is least tested, and the minority position, though speculative, is held by credible published work. A settled quantum-gravity account of the endpoint of evaporation, or direct observation, would resolve the question; neither exists.
